Fixing $\boldsymbol{\beta}_K = \mathbf{0}$ leaves $K-1$ vectors. Estimating all $K$ is the unconstrained softmax. The probabilities match. $K = 2$ with a zero reference class is binary logistic regression.

## Softmax, drawn

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$\mathbf{x}$$"] --> scores["$$\eta_k=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_k$$"]
  scores --> sm["softmax"]
  sm --> pi["$$\pi_k$$"]
  pi --> y["$$Y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$$"]
```

The class probabilities sum to 1. The cross-entropy is $-\sum_i\sum_k t_{ik}\log\pi_{ik}$, with $t_{ik}$ the 1-of-$K$ indicator.

::: {.notes}
Ordered categories are a cumulative model. Burakov notes them and stays with the unordered softmax.
:::

## The chapter, on this slide {#sec-burakov}

Denis Burakov, *Logistic Regression: From Maximum Likelihood to Machine Learning*, is the source of the loss, the weight-of-evidence arithmetic, and the softmax. The viewer scrolls the chapter.

{{< pdf references/burakov-logistic-regression.pdf width=100% height=500 >}}

## A Wald interval is a large-sample interval for $\pi$ {#sec-wald-pi}

Burakov builds the interval for a new covariate row $\mathbf{x}_0$ on the logit, then inverts it. The covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, with $w_i = \hat\pi_i(1-\hat\pi_i)$.

$$
\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \pm 1.96\sqrt{\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\,\mathbf{x}_0}.
$$

The endpoints are symmetric on the logit. After the inverse logit they sit inside $(0,1)$ and they are not symmetric on the probability scale. The justification is the asymptotic normality of the maximum-likelihood estimator. A small sample, or the perfect separation on the [checks figure](#sec-glm-checks), is outside that justification.

## A conformal interval uses a calibration set {#sec-conformal}

The same chapter then builds an interval whose coverage is finite-sample, under exchangeability, from a calibration set that was not used to fit $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Fit the logit on the training rows.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} On the calibration rows, score each residual. The Pearson form he uses is $(y - \hat\pi)/\sqrt{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)}$.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Add and subtract a quantile of those scores. On the logit scale the interval is symmetric around $\mathrm{logit}(\hat\pi)$, and the inverse logit brings it back to $(0,1)$ without clipping.

A classical conformal prediction set for a binary label is a set of classes. The interval here is for $\pi$. Whether the 0/1 outcome falls inside a narrow band for $\pi$ is a different question, and he treats it as the wrong coverage check.

## Hold the other covariates still

With several covariates,

$$
g(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots
$$

$\exp(\beta_1)$ is the multiplicative change in the mean, or in the odds, for a one-unit step in $x_1$ **with the other covariates held at the same values**.

If $x_2$ is a mediator or a collider, "held still" is a different estimand, not a more adjusted one.

## Ad hoc, post hoc, intrinsic {#sec-hoc}

[Qin Ma](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-025-02852-0) uses the three words for bioinformatics, and they transfer. An ad hoc analysis answers one question with one pre-chosen tool. A post hoc analysis, in that paper, reconciles several tools or several datasets after the fact. An intrinsic analysis builds the check into the model.

In this workshop "post hoc" also means the comparisons you make after a model that has more than two levels. Those are not the same operation. The next slides are the second meaning. Choosing the comparison because it was the significant one is [data dredging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_dredging): the hypothesis was suggested by the same data that are asked to confirm it.

## Contrasts from the model you fitted

When the groups and the covariates are in one model, the comparisons are contrasts from that fit. [Heiss](https://www.andrewheiss.com/blog/2022/05/20/marginalia/) separates two averages. An average marginal effect averages the contrast over the observed rows. A marginal effect at the mean evaluates it at the average covariate. `marginaleffects` defaults to the first. `emmeans` defaults to the second. They differ when the model is not linear.

Reporting several of those contrasts is still a family. The adjustment is simultaneous inference for the family you planned, not a correction chosen after the significant rows appear.

## A row of coefficients is a family {#sec-multiplicity}

$$
H_{0j}: \beta_j = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p.
$$

One row per coefficient hides that family. The matching statement is a joint region, or simultaneous intervals: Bonferroni intervals for a Bonferroni test, Tukey or Scheffé intervals for those contrast families. A logistic, Poisson, or negative-binomial model has the same family. The criterion does not change because the distribution did.

::: {.notes}
StatHarbor Analytics, *Multiple Testing Correction* (2026), from the slide "Multiplicity in Linear Models". Testing and interval estimation are dual: a family-wise procedure induces simultaneous intervals with joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\). Pointwise bands on a curve are the individual-test object; a simultaneous band is the corrected one.
:::

## The follow-up matches the family

After a global analysis of variance, name the contrasts before you test them.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} All pairwise means: Tukey.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Each treatment against a control: Dunnett.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Arbitrary contrasts: Scheffé, or simultaneous inference from the fitted model.

The correction belongs to that family. It is not a fee paid because several means exist.

## Genomics is a large exploratory family

A screen of thousands of genes, tens of thousands of proteins, or millions of variants is a different family. Missing a true signal is costly, and a controlled share of false leads is acceptable.

That is a false-discovery rate: Benjamini–Hochberg, an adaptive version, or a \(q\)-value. A \(q\)-value is not a posterior probability that the finding is true. A family-wise guarantee of no false claim at all spends power the screen cannot afford.

## One false claim, or some false signal

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} A family-wise error rate is the right target when even one false claim is costly.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} A false-discovery rate is the right target when the aim is broad discovery and some controlled false signal is acceptable.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Dependence, a hierarchy, or a structured set of contrasts often recovers power that a generic worst-case correction spends.

A procedure that controls the family-wise rate also controls the false-discovery rate, usually at that cost in power.

::: {.notes}
Because \(V \le R\) whenever \(R > 0\), the false-discovery rate is at most the family-wise error rate. Holm rejects every hypothesis Bonferroni rejects, for the same family and the same level. Questions before choosing: what is the family, is the setting confirmatory or exploratory, what false-positive burden is tolerable, and are the tests independent, positively dependent, or structured? Report the family, the criterion, the procedure, and the adjusted summary. Do not choose the correction after seeing which rows were small.
:::

## Which procedure for which family

| Scenario | Family | Typical procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary confirmatory endpoints | Small and prespecified | Holm, gatekeeping, closed testing |
| All pairwise means | Structured contrasts | Tukey HSD |
| Many genomic features | Very large, exploratory | Benjamini–Hochberg, adaptive BH, \(q\)-values |
| Complex dependence | Structured and correlated | Westfall–Young, or a bootstrap calibration |

Define the family and the error criterion before the claims. This grid is from StatHarbor Analytics, *Multiple Testing Correction* (2026).

## Two places to go next

[@bretzMultipleComparisonsUsing2016a] develops these procedures as maximum statistics and shows the R implementations. [@farcomeniReviewModernMultiple2008] reviews the false-discovery proportion, dependence among the statistics, and the genomic case.

## A table of counts is a log-linear model {#sec-loglinear}

[Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 10](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson10) models a contingency table by a Poisson GLM. The cell count is $Y_{ab} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$. The lesson is this log-linear model. Independence, with neither margin as the response, is

$$
\log \mu_{ab} = \alpha + \alpha_a + \alpha_b.
$$

## Independence, drawn

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  a["level $$a$$"] --> eta["$$\log\mu_{ab}=\alpha+\alpha_a+\alpha_b$$"]
  b["level $$b$$"] --> eta
  eta --> y["$$Y_{ab}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$$"]
```

The fitted counts are row total times column total over $n$, and every odds ratio equals 1. A logit model is the conditional distribution of one margin. This log-linear model is the joint distribution. Dummy coding changes the separate coefficients. Differences of coefficients, the log odds, stay put.

::: {.notes}
A logit-equivalent log-linear model includes every association among the predictors. The lesson contrasts R's dummy coding, first level set to 0, with the zero-sum constraint in `loglin()`. Expected counts do not depend on that choice.
:::

## A normal latent on the log mean {.fit-fig #sec-pln}

![The Poisson log-normal model: counts and covariates enter a latent Gaussian layer, the counts are Poisson given the latent, and the same layer is constrained for a known grouping, a mixture, a low-rank covariance, or a sparse precision.](figures/sources/poisson-log-normal.webp){fig-alt="Standard Poisson log-normal. Counts Y and covariates X enter a latent Z drawn normal with mean mu and covariance Sigma. Given Z, the counts are Poisson with mean exp of Z. The mean of Z is X times a coefficient matrix. Extensions constrain that mean for known classes or unknown groups, and constrain Sigma to low rank or to a sparse precision." width="96%"}

[Chiquet, Mariadassou, and Robin](https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2021.588292). The figure's $\mu$ is the mean of the latent Gaussian. Here that mean is $m$, and $\mu$ stays $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$.

## The Poisson log-normal drawing

$$
\mathbf{Z}_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mathbf{m}_i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}),
\quad
m_{i\ell} = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}_\ell,
\quad
Y_{i\ell}\mid Z_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(\exp(o_{i\ell}+Z_{i\ell})\right).
$$

Townes: replace the gamma prior on the rate by a log-normal. The normal is the distribution of $\log$ of the Poisson mean.

## The moments sit above the Poisson line {#sec-pln-moments}

Aitchison and Ho, as quoted by Chiquet, Mariadassou, and Robin, give the margin after integrating the latent:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) = \exp\!\left(o_{i\ell} + m_{i\ell} + \sigma_{\ell\ell}/2\right),
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y_{i\ell}) = \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) + \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell})^2\left(e^{\sigma_{\ell\ell}}-1\right).
$$

The variance exceeds the mean. The covariance of two features has the sign of $\sigma_{\ell\ell'}$. Given $\mathbf{Z}_i$, the features are independent, so the dependence lives in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Twice the effort adds $\log 2$ to the offset $o_{i\ell}$.

::: {.notes}
The likelihood has no closed form once $\mathbf{Z}$ is integrated out. The paper fits it by a variational approximation, in the R package `PLNmodels`. The four corners of the figure constrain either $\mathbf{m}$ (a known class, or a mixture) or $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ (low rank, or a sparse precision).
:::

## What these three models do not cover

- a zero-inflated count is the [mixture](#sec-count-zip) already named, and it sits outside the exponential family
- a composition is the [conditioning on the library size](#sec-multinomial-sum); a log-ratio, after a deliberate treatment of the zeros, is a further model
- a continuous flux: often a positive continuous distribution, or a Gaussian model on a scale you can defend
- dependence in space or in time: the design block is next

Quasi-Poisson is a variance fix, not a full likelihood. Use it only if you can say what the interval means.
